summary: A Central European country that was partitioned several times in its history, suffered devastating losses in World War II, and from 1989 led the democratization of Eastern Europe; it is known for Chopin and Copernicus.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 966 the Polish Duke Mieszko I was baptized, and Poland thereby adopted Latin Catholicism. At the end of the 18th century Poland was partitioned among Russia, Prussia and Austria, and under Orthodox Russia and Protestant Prussia, Catholicism became the core of Polish national identity. During World War II the Jews, who made up one tenth of the population, were almost entirely murdered, and after the war the westward shift of the borders and the removal of Germans and Ukrainians made Poland a religiously highly homogeneous Catholic country. Under communism the Church was a refuge for the opposition, and the election of Karol Wojtyła, Cardinal of Kraków, as Pope John Paul II in 1978 further inspired the Solidarity movement.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Although the communist regime (1945–1989) promoted atheism, the number of non-religious people remained very small because of the Church's role in the anti-communist movement. After democratization in 1989, and especially in the 2010s after Poland joined the European Union, church attendance among young people fell sharply; sexual abuse scandals among the clergy and the Church's political positions on issues such as abortion also alienated some, and the non-religious population has gradually grown, concentrated in large cities such as Warsaw.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Orthodox Christians are mainly Belarusian and Ukrainian minorities in the Białystok area of Podlasie in the east, whose ancestors had lived there since the time of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Border changes after World War II and the forced resettlement of Ukrainians in 1947 under Operation Vistula greatly reduced the Orthodox population, which today makes up only about 1%.

religion.background: Poland accepted Catholicism with the baptism of Mieszko I in 966. In the 16th century the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth was known for religious tolerance, and the Warsaw Confederation of 1573 guaranteed freedom to all denominations; it was home to the largest Jewish population in Europe. After the partitions of the late 18th century, Catholicism became a symbol of national identity. The Holocaust of World War II and postwar population transfers made Poland a religiously homogeneous, predominantly Catholic country; during the communist period the Church supported the democratic movement, and secularization has gradually accelerated since 1989.

ranking.name: Polish
ranking.description: Polish belongs to the West Slavic branch and developed gradually after the founding of the Polish state in the 10th century. In the 16th-century Renaissance, poets such as Jan Kochanowski wrote in Polish, laying the foundation of the standard language. During the partitions from the late 18th century to 1918, Russia and Prussia pursued policies of Russification and Germanization and banned Polish in schools, but Poles preserved the language through secret teaching. After World War II, population transfers made Poland a linguistically highly homogeneous country, and almost the whole country speaks Polish as its mother tongue.

ranking.name: Ukrainian
ranking.description: There was originally an indigenous Ukrainian minority in southeastern Poland, who were forcibly dispersed to the west and north in 1947 by Operation Vistula. Since 2014, and especially after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, millions of Ukrainian refugees and workers have come to Poland, making Ukrainian the second most commonly spoken language in Poland; it can be heard everywhere in cities such as Warsaw and Kraków.

ranking.name: Kashubian
ranking.description: Kashubian is the language of the Kashubians around Gdańsk in the north. It belongs to the West Slavic branch and is close to Polish but has its own grammar and vocabulary. In the 19th and 20th centuries it was regarded as a dialect of Polish and suppressed; in 2005 Poland's Act on National and Ethnic Minorities and on the Regional Language recognized it as a regional language, and some schools offer Kashubian classes.

language.history: The earliest written Polish sentence appears in the Book of Henryków of 1270. In the 16th century, printing and the Renaissance led Polish to replace Latin as the literary language, and in the time of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth it was also the common language of the nobility. During the partitions of 1795–1918 the language became a tool of national resistance, and the 1901 school strike of schoolchildren in Września was a protest against German-language religious instruction. After Poland regained independence in 1918, Polish became the national language, and population changes after World War II made Poland a linguistically homogeneous country.

ranking.name: Pierogi
ranking.description: Dough wrapped around fillings of potato and cheese, sauerkraut and mushrooms, meat or fruit, pinched into half-moons and boiled, sometimes then fried with butter and onions, and served with sour cream.
ranking.history: Pierogi appeared in Poland as early as around the 13th century; legend says they were brought back from Kievan Rus' by Saint Hyacinth, and the name 'pierogi' derives from an Old Slavic word for 'feast'. Those filled with potato and cheese are called 'Russian pierogi' (ruskie), where 'ruskie' refers to the historical region of Red Ruthenia (today western Ukraine). Christmas Eve dinner contains no meat, hence the tradition of pierogi filled with sauerkraut and mushrooms.

ranking.name: Bigos (hunter's stew)
ranking.description: Sauerkraut and fresh cabbage are stewed for days with pork, beef, game, sausage, dried mushrooms and prunes; the more it is reheated, the more flavorful it becomes, with a rich, sour and savory taste.
ranking.history: The origins of bigos go back to the Middle Ages; legend says that kings of Poland–Lithuania cooked the dish from their quarry while hunting, hence the name. Sauerkraut was an important source of vitamins in the cold winter. In the 19th century the poet Adam Mickiewicz described bigos in his epic Pan Tadeusz, making it a symbol of Polish national culture. It is a common dish at Christmas and New Year gatherings.

ranking.name: Żurek (sour rye soup)
ranking.description: A sour soup made from a fermented rye flour base with white sausage, smoked meat, potatoes and boiled eggs, flavored with garlic and marjoram, sometimes served in a hollowed-out bread bowl.
ranking.history: Żurek is one of the oldest soups in Poland. In the Middle Ages it was regarded as food for the poor and for Lent, since meat was forbidden during Lent and people fed themselves on fermented rye soup. Traditionally, at the end of Lent a ceremony of 'burying żurek' was held to celebrate the coming of Easter. Today it is an essential Easter breakfast dish, and the white sausage and eggs from the food baskets blessed in church before Easter are added to the soup.

ranking.name: Gołąbki (stuffed cabbage rolls)
ranking.description: Blanched cabbage leaves are wrapped around a filling of minced meat, rice and onion, arranged in a pot and simmered until tender in tomato sauce or mushroom sauce.
ranking.history: Similar dishes exist throughout Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and stuffed cabbage is generally thought to have reached Poland in the late Middle Ages under the influence of Ottoman stuffed dishes. The name 'gołąbki' means 'little pigeons', and legend links it to a noble dish stuffed with pigeon meat. In Poland it is a traditional dish for family gatherings, weddings and the period around Christmas, with fillings varying slightly from region to region.

ranking.name: Pączki (Polish doughnuts)
ranking.description: Rich yeast dough filled with rose petal jam, plum jam or custard and deep-fried, then dusted with powdered sugar or covered with icing, with a soft texture.
ranking.history: Pączki are closely tied to 'Fat Thursday' (Tłusty Czwartek) before Lent, when people used up the lard, sugar and eggs in their homes before Lent began. In the 16th century they were still a savory dough made with lard, and only after the 17th century did they gradually become today's sweet version. Today, on Fat Thursday each year, Poles eat hundreds of millions of doughnuts in a single day, and long queues form in front of bakeries.
